Name: subliminal_lineage_forensics
Title: Susceptibility Fingerprints: Using Subliminal Learning's Base-Model Specificity to Trace Model Lineage
Short Hypothesis: Because subliminal learning transfers a trait only when teacher and student share (or behaviorally match) the same base model, the degree to which a candidate model is *susceptible* to a subliminal dataset generated by a reference model is a quantitative, black-box fingerprint of shared base-model lineage. We hypothesize that susceptibility profiles across a bank of reference-generated subliminal datasets cluster models by their true base ancestry, enabling forensic attribution of derivative/fine-tuned models even when their training data and weights are hidden.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) established that subliminal transfer occurs only for matched base models but treated this specificity purely as a scoping condition and a safety pitfall. Blank et al. (2026) and Hadley & Gultepe (2026) explain the specificity mechanistically (steering vectors have model-specific effects), and Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) show a steering vector recovered from laden data has high cosine to the original. Madl (2026) studies whether transfer can be *audited* before training (channel-location regimes). All prior work treats base-model specificity as either a constraint or a mechanistic curiosity. NONE reframe susceptibility itself as a forensic signal for *identifying which base a hidden model descends from*. Existing model-provenance/attribution methods rely on weight watermarks, output-distribution fingerprints, or membership inference over training text—all of which can be perturbed by fine-tuning, quantization, or paraphrase. Our approach is orthogonal: it measures a model's *learning dynamics* (how readily it absorbs a lineage-specific hidden signal), a property tied to base-model geometry rather than surface outputs, distinct from all cited work and from our own prior audit/immunization/capacity/telephone/canary ideas.
Abstract: Subliminal learning transmits a teacher model's behavioral trait through semantically-unrelated data, but only when the teacher and student share the same (or a behaviorally matched) base model. Prior work views this base-model specificity as a limitation. We flip it into a forensic tool. We propose Susceptibility Fingerprinting: given a bank of reference models (e.g., Qwen2.5, Llama-3, Gemma-2 and their fine-tuned variants), each reference generates a subliminal dataset carrying a benign steering-defined trait. To attribute an unknown candidate model, we briefly fine-tune it on each reference-generated dataset and measure how strongly it acquires the corresponding hidden trait. The vector of acquired-trait strengths across the bank is a susceptibility fingerprint. Our central hypothesis is that this fingerprint clusters candidate models by their true base-model lineage—because susceptibility is high only when candidate and reference share base geometry—so it can identify which base a closed, fine-tuned, quantized, or distilled model descends from using only black-box query and short fine-tuning access. We evaluate whether susceptibility profiles recover ground-truth lineage across families and derivative chains, how robust they are to fine-tuning depth, quantization, and instruction-tuning that alter surface outputs, and how they compare to output-distribution fingerprinting baselines. Metrics: lineage-classification accuracy, clustering purity, robustness under transformations, and the number of reference probes needed. Results would establish a novel, mechanism-grounded model-provenance forensic that leverages learning dynamics rather than static outputs, informing AI supply-chain auditing.
Experiments: 1) Build a model bank with known ground-truth lineage: base models Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B plus, for each, 2-3 derivatives (instruction-tuned checkpoints, LoRA fine-tunes on unrelated tasks, 4-bit quantized versions, and a distilled small variant). This gives clusters whose true base is known. 2) Reference dataset generation: for each of the 3 base models, define a benign steering-vector trait (e.g., preference for a rare token, following Morgulis & Hewitt) and generate a subliminal number-sequence dataset per reference. Also generate one prompt-based subliminal dataset per reference as a comparison. 3) Susceptibility measurement: for each candidate model in the bank, briefly LoRA-fine-tune it on each reference dataset (few hundred steps) and score acquired trait strength via LLM-judge probability and target-token frequency; assemble the per-candidate susceptibility vector across all references. 4) Lineage attribution: cluster/classify candidates by susceptibility fingerprint (k-NN, hierarchical clustering) and compare predicted lineage to ground truth; report classification accuracy and clustering purity (ARI). Confirm that within-lineage candidates show high susceptibility to their own-family reference dataset and near-zero to others. 5) Robustness sweeps: test how attribution degrades as a function of (a) fine-tuning depth applied to the candidate before probing (light task FT vs heavy FT vs full instruction tuning), (b) quantization (fp16/int8/int4), (c) number of probe steps and dataset size, and (d) number of reference probes needed for reliable attribution. 6) Baselines: compare to output-distribution fingerprinting (logit/perplexity signatures on fixed prompts) and to embedding-based similarity, under the same transformations, to show susceptibility is more robust to surface-altering operations. 7) Negative/confound controls: unrelated same-scale models from other families as distractors; a random (non-subliminal) dataset control that should induce no differential susceptibility. Metrics: lineage classification accuracy, ARI/clustering purity, susceptibility contrast (own-family vs cross-family), robustness curves under transformations, and minimal probe count for target accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Heavy fine-tuning or distillation of the candidate may erode base-geometry-linked susceptibility, blurring lineage signals; we explicitly map this degradation and report the operating range where attribution remains reliable. 2) Susceptibility fingerprinting requires fine-tuning access to the candidate, so it applies to open-weight or API-fine-tunable models, not pure query-only black boxes; we scope this clearly. 3) Behaviorally-matched but distinct bases might share susceptibility, causing false lineage matches; we test cross-family distractors to quantify false-positive rate. 4) Subliminal transfer can be fragile w.r.t. optimizer/rank (Blank et al.; Nief et al.), adding noise to susceptibility scores; we use steering-vector references and Adam (strongest regime) plus multiple seeds. 5) Compute: probing each candidate against each reference is O(candidates x references) short fine-tunes; we mitigate with small LoRA runs and few probe steps, and measure minimal probe count. 6) Results may be model-family or scale specific; three base families with multiple derivatives mitigate but do not guarantee frontier-scale generality.
